This activity demonstrates a procedure for finding the inverse of a matrix $A$.

Suppose that $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \amp -2 \\ 1 \amp -1 \\ \end{bmatrix} $. To find an inverse $B$, we write its columns as $B = \begin{bmatrix}\bvec_1 \amp \bvec_2 \end{bmatrix}$ and require that $$ \begin{aligned} AB \amp = I \\ \begin{bmatrix} A\bvec_1 \amp A\bvec_2 \end{bmatrix} \amp = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}. \end{aligned} $$ In other words, we can find the columns of $B$ by solving the equations $$ A\bvec_1 = \twovec10,~~~ A\bvec_2 = \twovec01. $$ Solve these equations to find $\bvec_1$ and $\bvec_2$. Then write the matrix $B$ and verify that $AB=I$. This is enough for us to conclude that $B$ is the inverse of $A$.

Find the product $BA$ and explain why we now know that $B$ is invertible and $B^{-1}=A$.

What happens when you try to find the inverse of $C = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \amp 1 \\ 4 \amp -2 \\ \end{bmatrix}$?

We now develop a condition that must be satisfied by an invertible matrix. Suppose that $A$ is an invertible $n\times n$ matrix with inverse $B$ and suppose that $\bvec$ is any $n$-dimensional vector. Since $AB=I$, we have $$ A(B\bvec) = (AB)\bvec = I\bvec = \bvec. $$ This says that the equation $A\xvec = \bvec$ is consistent and that $\xvec=B\bvec$ is a solution.

Since we know that $A\xvec = \bvec$ is consistent for any vector $\bvec$, what does this say about the span of the columns of $A$?

Since $A$ is a square matrix, what does this say about the pivot positions of $A$? What is the reduced row echelon form of $A$?

In this activity, we have studied the matrices $$ A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \amp -2 \\ 1 \amp -1 \\ \end{bmatrix},~~~ C = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \amp 1 \\ 4 \amp -2 \\ \end{bmatrix}. $$ Find the reduced row echelon form of each and explain how those forms enable us to conclude that one matrix is invertible and the other is not.
